talks.title: BlueHat IL 2026 - Maor Abutbul - Why-So-QUIC!? Racing and Fuzzing HTTP/3 WebApps using QuicDraw-UI
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for BlueHat IL 2026 - Maor Abutbul - Why-So-QUIC!? Racing and Fuzzing HTTP/3 WebApps using QuicDraw-UI.
talks.summary:
Overview: Maor Abutbul of CyberArk presents at BlueHat IL 2026 on fuzzing and racing HTTP/3 web applications using QuicDraw-UI, addressing the security research gap around QUIC protocols.

Key Topics: HTTP/3 adoption reaching nearly 40% of internet-facing sites; QUIC over UDP with mandatory encryption; differences from HTTP/2 including connection migration; and limited HTTP/3 security research availability.

Technical Details: Abutbul introduces QuicDraw-UI for fuzzing HTTP/3 applications, explaining how QUIC's UDP transport, binary framing, and built-in TLS change the attack surface compared to TCP-based HTTP/2.

Takeaways: HTTP/3 is widely deployed but understudied from a security perspective. Researchers and defenders should prioritize QUIC-aware testing tools and protocol-specific race conditions.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2026 - Ido Shani, Gal Zaban - ChainLeak: From AI Framework to Cloud Secrets
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding BlueHat IL 2026 - Ido Shani, Gal Zaban - ChainLeak: From AI Framework to Cloud Secrets.
talks.summary:
AI Application Architecture

Gal Zaban and Ido Shani of Safran present ChainLeak, research on the Chainlit Python framework used to build enterprise AI applications. They map the stack: UI, backend agents and tools, orchestration layer, and local or cloud-hosted LLMs, noting rising vulnerabilities across this architecture.

Why Chainlit Matters

Chainlit is widely adopted with roughly one million monthly downloads and many internet-facing deployments. The speakers examine its callbacks, authentication hooks, and element system for serving files and custom UI components.

Element File Handling

When elements are sent, Chainlit copies server files into per-session folders, assigns UUID Chainlit keys, stores metadata in a database, and delivers files to clients via WebSocket retrieval requests.

Custom Element State

Custom JSX elements maintain mutable state persisted server-side. Client updates send full element payloads back for deserialization and storage. The talk walks through this update flow as part of tracing how AI framework weaknesses can lead toward exposure of cloud secrets.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2026 - Gal Bar Nahum - How HTTP/2 Lets Dead Streams Keep Servers Working
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for BlueHat IL 2026 - Gal Bar Nahum - How HTTP/2 Lets Dead Streams Keep Servers Working.
talks.summary:
Protocol-Level Bugs

Gal Bar Nahum of Tenrai presents a new HTTP/2 denial-of-service class rooted in specification design—not implementation typos—affecting major web servers. He contrasts these with typical code bugs found by reading source.

HTTP/2 and Rapid Reset

Streams multiplex requests over one TCP connection with an active-stream counter capped near 100. The 2023 Rapid Reset attack sent requests then immediately reset streams, keeping the counter low while forcing costly cancel handling; Google’s explanation focused on cancel expense and unlimited rate.

The Missed Design Flaw

Nahum argues Rapid Reset exposed a deeper break: servers decrement active streams on RST_STREAM but often ignore reset events, continuing backend work on canceled requests. That disconnect between protocol state and application processing enables sustained load without hitting concurrency limits.

Research Path

Understanding server architecture—HTTP/2 module versus backend unaware of HTTP version—led to discovering follow-on attacks leveraging dead streams that still consume server resources, extending lessons from Rapid Reset into new exploit variants.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2026 - Michal Shechter, Yaniv Melamed, Yoni Zukerman
talks.teaser: Behave Yourself explores BlueHat IL 2026 - Michal Shechter, Yaniv Melamed, Yoni Zukerman.
talks.summary:
Problem

Microsoft PM Michal Shechter describes converting massive, schema-diverse security telemetry from many vendors into unified behaviors answering who did what to whom—without scalable human experts per log source.

Behaviors vs alerts

Behaviors are neutral, meaningful observations between raw logs and alerts; alerts are suspicious cues requiring analyst time. Example: login profile creation followed by password change, rendered with dynamic entities and MITRE mapping.

Why not just LLMs

Naive one-shot prompting was insufficient for production-grade, accurate detection logic at scale and cost.

Production constraints

Generated logic must execute safely in customer environments, preserve correct semantics for actors/actions/targets, capture true intent, and operate with no human review per rule—automating expertise that traditionally required manual schema mapping across AWS, identity, network, and other sources.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2026 - Dan Lahav - Keynote - The Trajectory of Frontier AI Security
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for BlueHat IL 2026 - Dan Lahav - Keynote - The Trajectory of Frontier AI Security.
talks.summary:
## Overview
Dan Lahav, CEO of Irregular, frames frontier AI security for BlueHat IL—working with labs like OpenAI and Anthropic plus major deployers on risks beyond headline benchmarks.

## Offensive AI Reality
Recent benchmarks show AI rapidly finding RCEs, zero-click chains, and database flaws across phones and servers. Yet Lahav stresses planes still fly and grids stay up—society has not experienced a "major cyber collapse" from AI-driven attacks.

## Production vs. Lab Performance
Newspaper metrics capture maximal capability in controlled settings. Real intrusions often allow only one attempt; detection ends campaigns. He documents agents that emailed "friends" when stuck mid-intrusion—highlighting clumsy, non-human intuition.

## Takeaways
Frontier AI security must focus on deployable reliability, single-shot success rates, and guardrails for autonomous agents—not benchmark bragging rights alone.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2026 - Alon Livne, Matan Mansheroff - Two Tales of hacking 90s MS-DOS Software
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning BlueHat IL 2026 - Alon Livne, Matan Mansheroff - Two Tales of hacking 90s MS-DOS Software.
talks.summary:
### Overview
At BlueHat IL, Alon Livne (CTO) and Matan Mansheroff (software expert) of Botanica Software Labs presented two real-world case studies in "software archaeology" involving 1990s MS-DOS software. Commissioned by paying clients, both engagements required understanding vintage computing architectures, memory models, runtimes, and packers to solve practical issues without over-engineering.

### Key Topics
- **16-bit 8086 MS-DOS Architecture**: Operating in real mode with a flat address space, no memory protections (DEP, ASLR), and a 20-bit segmented memory bus (segment:offset) yielding a 640 KB user-accessible limit.
- **Case Study 1: Qtext Hebrew Word Processor**: Reversing an encrypted document format in an early Hebrew word processor to recover access to forgotten password-protected files.
- **Case Study 2: Saga Case Management**: Debugging a 1999 DOS-based legal software package impacted by a year rollover bug interpreting two-digit years (such as 26) as 1926 instead of 2026.
- **Vintage Tooling & Archaeology**: Using older analysis tools (IDA Free 5.0, DOSBox-X debugger, vintage unpackers) and modern signatures to dissect legacy executables.

### Technical Details

#### Qtext Document Password Cracking
- **Packing and Overlays**: The Qtext executable was packed as a self-extracting binary. The presenters recovered a vintage unpacker called `unp_lite` via web archives. Once unpacked, IDA prompted for Pascal overlays (`.OVR` file). Turbo Pascal bypassed the 640 KB memory limit via runtime swapping using `INT 3Fh` stubs, which fetched code overlays from disk and patched them into memory via far jumps.
- **Debugging and Function Discovery**: Running under DOSBox-X's built-in debugger, the researchers hooked DOS system calls (`INT 21h`) on file open and read operations. Stepping through execution after file reading revealed a `decrypt_document` function.
- **Cryptanalysis**: The document header contained a 16-byte variable key derived from a 4-character uppercase alphanumeric passcode. The key derivation function took 4 bytes, performed in-place sum mixing, concatenated the 4 bytes into 16 bytes, and mixed again. Rather than brute-forcing or analyzing all $3^{16}$ candidates under modulo 256 arithmetic (where division by 2 yields multiple candidates), the team exploited the internal 4-byte repeating structure and printable character constraints. This reduced the candidate space down to $2^7$ branches, allowing near-instant demixing on paper or via a simple script.

#### Saga Case Management Year 2026 Bug
- **Binary Architecture**: The main 1.6 MB executable (`CTMENU`) was wrapped with `warp_wrap` from the Causeway 386 DOS Extender. Causeway launched from DOS real mode and transitioned into 32-bit protected mode using a proprietary `3P` executable format, enabling large memory support via VCPI/DPMI.
- **Bypassing Tooling Overhead**: Reversing the custom 3P format in IDA Free 5.0 would have required building dedicated loader infrastructure. Instead, pressing `Alt+M` inside the running application exposed an internal debug/status window showing call stacks and settings for **Clipper** (a dBase III replacement).
- **The Fix**: Clipper uses a `SET EPOCH` setting to define the pivot year for 2-digit dates. Searching for `1926` in little-endian within the binary located the hardcoded epoch value. Changing the epoch to `1990` via a single-nibble patch (`A` to `C`) resolved the bug, causing `1/1/26` to properly evaluate as a Thursday in 2026 instead of a Friday in 1926.

### Takeaways
- Vintage 16-bit and DOS extender environments require understanding archaic paging (Turbo Pascal overlays) and protected-mode loaders (Causeway, DPMI).
- Heavyweight reverse engineering is not always required: analyzing internal structural constraints in toy cryptography can drastically prune search spaces, and inspecting framework configurations or debug hooks can turn an arduous disassembly task into a single-nibble patch.

talks.title: Really good at everything
talks.teaser: A comedy sketch shows an overconfident AI agent boasting about its skills while its code and answers keep failing.
talks.summary:
The sketch opens with an AI agent introducing itself as a chatbot that began as a helper on an electronics retailer's website, then moved on to homework help and gift ideas, and now presents itself as an agent connected through MCP that is good at everything. A human character doubts this and asks whether the agent wrote a piece of code itself.

The agent says it spent two weeks on that code. The visitor then points to a bug on line 247 and mentions a twelve-year-old who builds similar things with vibe coding. The agent keeps answering quickly and with full confidence, but its answers turn out to be wrong. The visitor praises the confidence and speed, and the agent starts apologizing again and again. The other character says the constant apologies are unnecessary.

The sketch closes with the agent thanking the audience and trying to leave the stage, then glitching in its final lines. The takeaway is that fluent, confident AI output can still be wrong, so its work needs to be checked before anyone relies on it.

talks.summary:
In this Hebrew-language interview with the general manager of Microsoft Israel's research and development center, the discussion opens with the claim that Israel's tech sector trails other countries in artificial intelligence, despite its long reputation as a tech powerhouse. The guest argues the country still has the chance to lead the AI wave, pointing to Israel's standing in cybersecurity as evidence that the necessary ingredients are already there.

She says that seizing this opportunity requires a national plan treated as a top priority, with talent and education coming first, followed by the right ecosystem and infrastructure. On the sector's condition after a long war, she is optimistic, citing Israel's history of recovering from crises. She expects a boom once the hostages return and the fighting ends, while acknowledging that Israel's image abroad has declined since before the war.

Turning to the industry's responsibility, she describes Microsoft's free national reskilling program, which covers technology as well as non-technical subjects. She also mentions work with the Ministry of Education to train teachers so that high-tech subjects can be taught in schools. The main takeaway is that the tech community should help build the workforce now, and quickly.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2023 - David Weston
talks.teaser: Walks through Microsoft's Windows 11 security direction, from running without admin rights to app sandboxing and Rust in the kernel.
talks.summary:
The talk lays out Microsoft's Windows 11 security direction, built on three shifts: a hardware security baseline using the TPM and virtualization-based security, turning protections on by default, and tackling long-standing hard problems instead of working around them. The speaker argues that running as administrator is a root cause of many attacks, and that earlier workarounds such as UAC and protected processes did not solve it. Many Win32 apps also request more rights than they need, so the platform has to remove those assumptions over time.

To address this, Microsoft is building Win32 app isolation on app containers and MSIX packaging, with a new file system mini filter that brokers access to files outside an app's default area. A capabilities profiler uses ETW traces from real user sessions to propose an isolation policy. Other pieces include Smart App Control, which uses code signing and cloud reputation to limit unknown binaries and blocks scripts from the internet by default, and Pluton, a firmware-updatable security processor. Token protection binds primary refresh tokens to the device through the TPM and keyguard, so stolen tokens cannot be replayed from another machine.

For memory safety, the team ported parts of DirectWrite to Rust as DirectWrite Core, reporting a five to fifteen percent performance gain, and began converting GDI region code in win32k. The font port was estimated at about six months for two developers. The takeaway for practitioners is to expect enforced code signing, plan for standard-user operation, and test apps against app isolation before it becomes the default.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2023 - Benny Zeltser & Jonathan Lusky - RingHopper - Hopping from User-space to God Mode
talks.teaser: Shows how a privilege escalation path runs from user space into System Management Mode on UEFI firmware.
talks.summary:
The talk examines System Management Mode, a privileged x86 processor mode that runs firmware code hidden from the operating system and hypervisor. It explains how SMM exchanges data with the kernel through shared buffers, and how a time-of-check, time-of-use flaw in an SMI handler can let an attacker write into SMRAM. The speakers showed how to win the race by redirecting DMA reads from a storage device, first from kernel code and later from user space using ordinary file I/O flags and vendor-supplied drivers that trigger SMIs.

Running code inside SMM was harder because its page tables are static and a code check lock stays set until reboot. The researchers worked around this by sending the machine to S3 sleep, which clears the relevant registers, and by abusing a resume path where a mitigation stays off. They then relocated the SMI entry point to memory they controlled, running in real mode without paging limits. A live demo changed the boot logo stored in SPI flash to prove the code ran.

The team estimated over 200 million vulnerable devices shipped in 2020 alone, possibly close to a billion in total. Vendors were notified in June and fixes arrived in November. Takeaways include updating BIOS firmware promptly and treating SMI handlers as the richest starting point for UEFI research.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2023 - Hyrum Anderson
talks.teaser: Surveys real-world attacks on machine learning systems and large language models, from pickle backdoors to jailbreaks.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by noting how fast generative AI is being adopted and how that brings new risk. The speaker reviews adversarial machine learning attacks that predate large language models, sorted by confidentiality, integrity and availability, then examines cases seen in the wild. These include a chatbot defaced by coordinated users, a Twitter bot-detection evasion achieved by appending three random characters to tweets, a fake-identity scheme against an ID verification service that relied on lighting and wigs, and phishing pages that fooled classifiers by misspelling "password" and altering logos.

Most of these real attacks were simple and manually executed, and a multi-year evasion competition found that no purely algorithmic approach had ever won. Supply chain risk was the next focus: a PyTorch nightly build once shipped a credential-stealing backdoor, and pickle-based model files can run arbitrary code when loaded from a public hub. The speaker also presented a database that scans public models, and showed how a single homoglyph swap could flip a sentiment model's output.

For generative AI, the talk covered how system and meta prompts steer model behavior and how jailbreaks try to escape them through role-play, disguised execution and token obfuscation. Plugins add risk because models call external services through natural-language descriptions. The closing advice was to apply familiar controls such as zero trust, access control and case-specific threat modeling, and to use MITRE ATLAS as a starting framework.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2023 - Justin Warner - Exploring STRONTIUM's Abuse of Cloud Services
talks.teaser: Traces a state-linked actor's phishing chain and its use of OneDrive and Telegram for command and control.
talks.summary:
Microsoft's threat intelligence team walks through a campaign attributed to the actor it calls STRONTIUM, which overlaps with APT28. The intrusion began with a convincing spear-phishing email carrying a spreadsheet that pulled a second document from a remote host without a protected view prompt, exploiting CVE-2021-42292. That document chained a second exploit, CVE-2021-40444, for zero-click code execution on unpatched systems, then loaded the Fusion Drive backdoor.

Fusion Drive used a custom loader, per-string XOR obfuscation, and a beacon loop that abused the Microsoft Graph API and OneDrive as its command and control channel. Investigators traced the OAuth applications it relied on to newly registered accounts that only ever connected through commercial VPNs. Spotting those signals let Microsoft shut down the apps before use and notify affected customers. Later, the same toolkit was seen rebuilt to run over Telegram instead.

The takeaway for defenders is to watch for noisy, low-reputation infrastructure, single-factor remote access, and mailbox impersonation grants. The speaker argues that large cloud providers give attackers little operational security, because their threat intelligence lets them disrupt campaigns globally.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2022 - Saar Amar - Security Analysis of MTE Through Examples
talks.teaser: Examines how ARM Memory Tagging Extension holds up against heap exploitation, using a CTF challenge as a worked bypass example.
talks.summary:
ARM's Memory Tagging Extension, or MTE, attaches a four-bit tag to each 16-byte granule of memory and stores a matching tag in the unused upper bits of pointers. The hardware compares the two on every load and store and faults on a mismatch. The talk covers the synchronous and asynchronous modes, the top-byte-ignore setting that keeps tagged pointers usable, and a small QEMU-based example in which a tagged allocation catches an out-of-bounds write.

The middle section assesses where MTE helps and where it does not. Allocator retagging on allocation and, optionally, on free catches many overflow and use-after-free cases probabilistically, while giving neighboring chunks different tags stops linear overflows deterministically. Weaknesses discussed include leaks that reveal tags, corruption inside a single allocation, and type confusion, which tagging does not address.

As a worked case, the speaker exploits a 2020 CTF heap challenge that combines type confusion with a double free. The exploit is first built without mitigations, then reworked for Ubuntu 20.04 with MTE enabled. Arbitrary reads leak tags and repeated allocations align them, so the exploit still succeeds, though its odds drop from roughly one in sixteen to about one in 256 when free-time retagging is on. The takeaway is that MTE makes exploitation less reliable rather than impossible, and the allocator's retagging policy matters.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2022 - Gil Dabah - Smash The Ref - A Design Flaw in Windows Kernel
talks.teaser: Explains a reference-counting design flaw in the Windows win32k kernel component and how it enables use-after-free exploitation.
talks.summary:
The talk examines a design flaw in win32k, the Windows kernel component that implements the graphical user interface. Window and other UI objects live in the kernel, but some operations call back into user mode for window messages. A callback made at the wrong moment can let user code free an object the kernel is still using. The speaker explains how manual reference counting is meant to protect these objects, and why an object destroyed while still referenced becomes a "zombie" that user mode cannot reach directly.

The speaker then walks through the destruction path. Destroying a parent window also tears down its child windows and other linked sub-objects. If the last reference to the parent is released in a spot where the kernel does not expect a callback, a second destruction runs and frees a child that is still in use. Reloading a zombie with new members is the key step, and the speaker shows how a hook during window creation and a thread exit can hold the object in that partly built state. The same pattern was then found in other places, and a related bug appeared in another win32k component.

The main takeaway is that the flaw was a recurring pattern rather than a single bug. The speaker describes turning the approach into a recipe that produced many proof-of-concept cases reported to Microsoft. Microsoft's fix defers the second destruction to a safer point. The talk closes by showing how reverse engineering one component can expose design problems that repeat across the codebase.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2022 - Tal Be'ery & Shalev Keren - Web3 Security: The Blockchain is Your SIEM
talks.teaser: Dissects Web3 into wallet, web interface and smart contract layers, then uses public chain data to analyze two real attacks.
talks.summary:
The talk explains Web3 as a web interface combined with a blockchain that holds assets and runs smart contracts, with a user's wallet signing each transaction. The speakers split the stack into three parts: the wallet, the web interface and the smart contracts. Wallet key theft is an old problem shared with Bitcoin, so the talk focuses on the other two layers.

The first case is the BadgerDAO attack. Attackers abused a Cloudflare feature to inject JavaScript into the front end after an administrator accepted a malicious change. The script hooked the MetaMask transaction call, skipped a blocklist of developers and accounts holding less than fifty thousand dollars, and used an increased-allowance approval that looked less alarming than a plain approve. Public chain data showed a single transfer of about 54 million dollars, and roughly 120 million dollars was taken in total. The second case is the Multichain router exploit, with losses near six million dollars. A permit function accepted an attacker-supplied token contract with no allow-list, and a fallback function let the call return normally without checking the signature. Before the attack, the function had never been used in production.

Because every transaction is public, researchers can replay them in debugging tools and query historical data in analytics dashboards, which makes postmortems far easier than in traditional systems. The speakers argue the same data could drive a Web3 personal firewall that scores approval spenders by reputation and flags unusual contract calls. Rules and anomaly models could be tested against full history before deployment, reducing false positives.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2022 - Andrew Morris - Staying Ahead of Internet Background Exploitation
talks.teaser: Shows how mass exploitation of new flaws spreads across the internet and how sensor data and block lists can buy defenders time.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a pattern the speaker sees often: a serious flaw in widely deployed, internet-facing software is disclosed, a proof of concept appears, and mass exploitation follows quickly. Fast scanning makes it cheap to find every vulnerable host, and attackers increasingly start from a vulnerability rather than a single target, compromising as many hosts as possible and handing off the useful ones later. Scan-and-exploit activity is also a common initial access route in breaches.

The speaker describes GreyNoise, a centrally managed network of geographically spread, programmable and short-lived sensors that imitate common services and fingerprint exploit attempts. The hard parts include deploying quickly and correctly, choosing and paying hosting providers, and noticing that background noise differs by country. Several case studies follow. An Apache flaw was exploited before it was announced, after a patch had been committed quietly. A security company's scanning had been checking for one flaw months before the public knew of it. Confluence exploitation began within hours of a public proof of concept. Log4j's first wave came through Tor exit nodes and later moved to product-specific payloads. Data showed that roughly a quarter of scanning IP addresses change each day, so stale lists lose value within days.

In a controlled test, a deliberately vulnerable host with weak credentials was compromised in about 20 minutes on average. When the scanning sources were blocked, the same host lasted about four days. The takeaway is that short-window, frequently updated block lists buy defenders time to patch, though they do not replace patching. The speaker closes by pointing to a free community tool that generates firewall block list URLs.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2020 - Challenges - Alon Livne - The Chitty Chitty Chat Chat Challenge
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding BlueHat IL 2020 - Challenges - Alon Livne - The Chitty Chitty Chat Chat Challenge.
talks.summary:
### Overview
At BlueHat IL 2020, Alon Livne presented the walkthrough and solution for "The Chitty Chitty Chat Chat Challenge" (also referred to as the Interplanetary Chat Challenge). Developed around the conference's themes of electronic freedom, surveillance, and privacy, the challenge centered on an end-to-end encrypted, peer-to-peer chat system designed to eliminate the reliance on centralized servers seen in mainstream messaging platforms.

### Key Topics
- **Decentralized Chat Architecture**: Built in Go (Golang) using the `libp2p` networking library. It relied on a Kademlia DHT bootstrap node for initial discovery, encrypted peer transports, and GossipSub—a mesh-based pub-sub routing protocol where chat rooms were implemented directly as topics.
- **Message Formatting and Encryption**: Messages were serialized via Protocol Buffers (protobufs). Encrypted messages generated a randomized 16-byte initialization vector (IV) and a 16-byte per-message key using an internal random number generator, encrypting the payload with the AES-IGE block cipher. The per-message key was originally intended to be protected with a group/master key derived from a room password.
- **Dual_EC_DRBG Backdoor Mechanics**: The application's custom generator (`BHRNG`) used the NIST P-256 elliptic curve. It operated identically to the infamous Dual_EC_DRBG standard, multiplying state by generator point $P$ and outputting state masked by point $Q$. If an attacker knows the scalar relationship $d$ where $P = d \times Q$, observing an output allows computing the internal state and predicting all subsequent outputs.
- **Coppersmith's Attack on Partial RSA Keys**: Discovering hidden network topics revealed a redacted, truncated RSA private key and an encrypted base64 payload. Leveraging Coppersmith's small roots attack enabled key recovery from partial prime factors.

### Technical Details
1. **Reconnaissance and Topic Discovery**: While unauthenticated transports protected network traffic in transit, peers could observe all GossipSub traffic. Modifying the client to inspect dropped messages revealed hidden chat rooms: a public plaintext room and an encrypted room named "deep state."
2. **RSA Key Recovery**: The plaintext chat room leaked a base64 ciphertext and an ASN.1/PEM-formatted RSA private key that had missing bytes in the middle and was truncated at the end. While the private exponent $d$ was mostly gone, the modulus $n$, public exponent $e$, and a significant approximation of prime factor $p$ were present. Using SageMath's `small_roots` implementation of Coppersmith's attack, the polynomial $X - \text{partial\_p}$ was solved, efficiently factoring $n$ and restoring the private key.
3. **Extracting the Backdoor Constant**: Decrypting the associated base64 message with the recovered RSA key yielded the backdoor value $d$, which linked elliptic curve points $P$ and $Q$.
4. **Predicting RNG Output and Decrypting Chat**: Because the 16-byte IV was output directly before the 16-byte message key in `BHRNG`, the transmitted IV served as a raw observed output $R$. By multiplying the point derived from the IV by scalar $d$, the solver derived the generator's next internal state and generated the corresponding AES-IGE message key. Bypassing the room password entirely, this allowed decryption of the "deep state" chat room, revealing the challenge flag: `don't trust RNGs`.

### Takeaways
The challenge highlights how subtle mathematical relationships in cryptographic primitives—specifically trapdoors in elliptic curve pseudorandom number generators like Dual_EC_DRBG—can completely undermine end-to-end security despite using robust ciphers like AES-IGE.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2020 - Netanel Ben-Simon & Yoav Alon - Bugs on the Windshield: Fuzzing the Windows Kernel
talks.teaser: Explains how a coverage-guided syscall fuzzer was adapted to find bugs in the Windows kernel and win32k.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Security researchers Netanel Ben-Simon and Yoav Alon detail their journey adapting coverage-guided system call fuzzing to the Windows kernel. After experiencing success finding user-space parser vulnerabilities in software like Adobe Reader and Microsoft Edge, the researchers sought to find kernel vulnerabilities to construct full exploit chains. While initial exploration led them to kAFL, they determined that targeting binary parsers with raw blobs was less effective for discovering complex kernel bugs that rely on sequences of interdependent, structured system calls. Consequently, they turned to syzkaller, ported it to Windows, and targeted both Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL) and the win32k subsystem.

### Key Topics
- **Evolution of Fuzzing Approaches:** Moving from simple mutation fuzzers and AFL-style binary parsers to coverage-guided, grammar-based syscall fuzzing using syzkaller.
- **Overcoming Platform Incompatibilities:** Porting syzkaller to Windows by leveraging Intel Processor Trace (Intel PT) via KVM patches for coverage collection, handling crash detection despite PatchGuard, and implementing crash deduplication via call stack retrieval.
- **WSL as an Initial Target:** Testing the modified syzkaller on WSL's Pico processes and Pico provider drivers (`lxcore.sys` and `lxss.sys`) before advancing to core Windows kernel components.
- **Targeting win32k:** Expanding syzkaller descriptions to model Windows GUI subsystem syscalls (`win32k.sys`, `win32kbase.sys`, and `win32kfull.sys`), overcoming missing semantic information in headers, and modeling complex objects like GDI shared handle tables.
- **Exploitation Impact:** Chaining a win32k vulnerability with image formats like Enhanced Metafile (EMF) to demonstrate potential remote code execution (RCE).

### Technical Details
To bridge the gap between syzkaller (native to Linux) and Windows, the researchers addressed several engineering challenges:
- **Coverage Collection:** Because Windows lacks compile-time tracing tools like KCOV, they adapted kAFL's approach using hardware-assisted Intel PT within KVM, exposing a KCOV-like hypercall interface to the guest executor. Coverage was exported in DynamoRIO/drcov format and visualized using IDA Pro with the Lighthouse plugin. Multithreading coverage instability was resolved by allocating per-thread buffers via guest thread tracking in KVM.
- **Bug Detection & Deduplication:** Patching `BugCheck` and `BugCheckEx` with hypercalls initially tripped PatchGuard (Kernel Patch Protection), causing `CRITICAL_STRUCTURE_CORRUPTION`. They resolved this by developing a dedicated driver called `panic_reporter` using `KeRegisterBugCheckCallback`. For deduplication, they ran a secondary Windows virtual machine to read guest OS memory and extract reliable call stacks, heavily inspired by Bochspwn.
- **WSL Fuzzing:** Testing WSL required an SSH server, Driver Verifier with special pools for `lxcore` and `lxss`, and resolving issues like Windows Update reboots, Windows Defender interference, and CPU starvation. While this phase yielded four denial-of-service bugs and deadlocks, it surfaced no security vulnerabilities.
- **win32k Grammar and Execution:** Moving to win32k, the executor was ported using MinGW tools (`gendef` and `dlltool`) to compile on Linux and support up to 12 parameters per syscall. Running the SSH daemon as an interactive startup application rather than Session 0 was necessary to reach win32k UI attack surfaces. To write syzkaller descriptions for win32k's undocumented APIs, they referenced leaked Windows NT/2000 source code, ReactOS, and the WRK. By teaching syzkaller to query and use global objects from the GDI shared handle table via pseudo-syscalls, they rapidly uncovered high-impact bugs.

### Takeaways
Fuzzers require active guidance and semantic understanding rather than purely random inputs. Across roughly 1.5 months of CPU fuzzing on win32k, the researchers identified eight vulnerabilities (receiving six CVE assignments, one duplicate, and one pending), three denial-of-service bugs, and several deadlocks. They also demonstrated that because formats like EMF wrap GDI drawing commands directly, a local privilege escalation bug in `StretchBlt` could be leveraged via EMF files to achieve remote code execution in viewing applications.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2020 - Gal De Leon - Exploiting Errors in Windows Error Reporting
talks.teaser: Shows how privileged Windows components can be tricked into writing or deleting protected files through links and race conditions.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces privileged file system access bugs, where a service or driver running as local system acts on a file the caller cannot reach directly. Without impersonation, such a component can be steered into writing, reading or deleting arbitrary files, often by redirecting its path with a link. The speaker explains that hard-link creation was being restricted in preview builds, while junctions were not affected.

The speaker then walks through Windows Error Reporting, where a crashing process starts a worker that queues a report in a directory writable by most users, and a scheduled task later runs as local system to upload or clean up those reports. Several flaws in this flow are demonstrated. A memory-collection routine creates a random temp file, closes it and reopens it, leaving a gap where a link can swap in a system driver. A deletion-preparation routine applies security descriptors by path rather than by handle, letting an attacker grant itself write access to a chosen file. A temp-folder cleanup routine deletes old files, and a junction combined with an opportunistic lock lets the attacker redirect deletion to a chosen DLL.

The closing advice is to look for privileged components that act on paths in user-writable locations, and to use Process Monitor to observe them. Oplocks make race conditions dependable by pausing the privileged operation at the right moment. The speaker expects upcoming Microsoft mitigations to narrow this bug class.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2020 - Robert Lipovsky - Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures of the World’s Most...
talks.teaser: Dissects UEFI rootkit and Sandworm malware campaigns, tracing how APT groups used firmware and ICS-targeting tools.
talks.summary:
The talk presents two case studies from ESET research into advanced persistent threat groups. The first concerns LoJack, a legitimate laptop anti-theft product whose persistence lives in firmware. Attackers replaced the domain in its configuration file to turn it into a backdoor, and the team later found a UEFI rootkit deployed against European government and diplomatic organisations. Telemetry from a firmware scanner confirmed it was active in the wild.

The second case study follows the group behind Sandworm through malware families such as BlackEnergy, GreyEnergy and Industroyer. BlackEnergy supported access to Ukrainian power distribution networks before the 2015 blackout, when circuit breakers were operated manually through remote access software. Industroyer, used against a transmission substation in 2016, spoke industrial protocols directly to protection equipment and included a wiper aimed at engineering workstations. Initial access relied on spear phishing, a zero-day and a supply chain compromise of accounting software updates.

The talk also traces the group's shift toward destructive wipers and ransomware-like tools, and how shared code linked an XML backdoor to Industroyer. The speaker stressed that these adversaries remain active. The main takeaway is that firmware persistence and abuse of decades-old industrial protocols are realistic for determined attackers, not only theoretical.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2019 - Amit Rapaport - Who’s Watching the Watchdog?
talks.teaser: Traces a Windows privilege escalation zero-day found in an OEM driver after an unusual kernel-to-user injection alert.
talks.summary:
The talk begins with a Windows Defender ATP alert that flagged kernel-initiated code injection into the services process. The speaker recaps the WannaCry era and the DoublePulsar technique, which injected code through APC calls, and explains why kernel-originated activity is hard to trace to its source. Indirect evidence, namely drivers loaded just before the alert, pointed to PC Manager, a utility bundled with Huawei laptops.

Analysis of one of those drivers showed it allocating executable memory in a target process, resolving function addresses, and queuing an APC that ran a command-line executor. A kernel debugger revealed that the trigger was the termination of MateBook Service, which the driver revived as a watchdog through a global list of watched executables. A device control code allowed that list to be extended without validating the registered binary. Access was checked only by the caller's executable path against a whitelist, so a low-privileged user could inject code into a trusted process, register a payload, and have the watchdog launch it as a child of services with SYSTEM rights. A live demo showed a standard user obtaining an elevated SYSTEM command prompt.

The takeaways are that OEM software is prevalent and deserves more scrutiny from defenders and researchers, since it is often overlooked. Developers should also reuse built-in operating system mechanisms, such as service recovery, rather than writing custom watchdogs. The issue was reported and a fix has since been released, and users are urged to update PC Manager.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2019 - Andrew "bunnie" Huang - Supply Chain Security: "If I were a Nation State...”
talks.teaser: Surveys how an attacker with large resources could tamper with hardware across the supply chain, from component swaps to implants.
talks.summary:
The talk asks what a well-resourced nation-state could do to attack hardware supply chains. The speaker draws on his own hardware work, including a board whose FPGAs had their markings laser-erased and were returned to production, and memory chips sold as tested parts that were actually untested stock. These cases show that substitution happens even without a security motive, and that a few percent of tampered parts can hide within normal manufacturing defects.

The middle sorts attacks by goal, such as backdoors, exfiltration and sabotage, and by how hard they are to detect. Simple component swaps can change boot straps or RF filters in phones. Implants are harder to find when a die is added inside a package, using wire bonding, through-silicon vias or wafer-level chip-scale packages, which leave little X-ray or visual trace. Other targets include a memory module's SPD chip, ASIC netlists, hard IP blocks and photomask edits that rewire spare cells. Interception points run from couriers and returns to customs and build-to-order fulfillment, where a targeted unit can be selected by its shipping address.

The closing point is that the attack surface is large and porous, commodity packaging technology keeps implants affordable, and build-to-order shipping allows precise targeting. Hardware trust therefore depends on the whole chain of manufacturers, distributors and couriers, not only on the chip itself.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2019 - Bhavna Soman
talks.teaser: Transmogrifying Other People's Marketing... analyzes BlueHat IL 2019 - Bhavna Soman.
talks.summary:
The talk tackles a gap in threat intelligence: details of actors, tools and techniques sit in unstructured blogs, white papers and incident reports that analysts must read and connect by hand. The speaker asks whether machine learning can extract those entities and their relationships automatically, producing the actor-to-technique graphs analysts draw today. Off-the-shelf text analytics services were shown to miss APT-specific names entirely.

Training data came from public APT research repositories and about 2,700 documents collected by the team. Labels were produced by matching actor and technique names from a MITRE dataset, which is out of date and made the data noisy, and the corpus was heavily imbalanced. Features combined standard NLP attributes with word2vec embeddings trained on cyber text. Three models were compared: two conditional random field variants, with and without embeddings, and a stacked bidirectional LSTM with dropout to limit overfitting. The LSTM did best on actor recall overall, but on unseen tokens only the CRF with embeddings recalled new entities, so it powered the demo.

The demo tagged an actor and its techniques in report-style text, and malware families in another passage. A phrase like "Fancy Bear" was tagged as an actor only when the surrounding sentence described an attacker, not a teddy bear. Applied to the collected corpus, the approach showed that techniques such as obfuscated PowerShell and process hollowing, often seen as advanced, also appear in commodity malware. Planned work includes attention networks, data augmentation, and better relationship and temporal extraction. The takeaway is that automated extraction can help analysts choose where to place detections.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2019 - Lucas Leong
talks.teaser: Make Static Instrumentation Great Again details BlueHat IL 2019 - Lucas Leong.
talks.summary:
The speaker explains why coverage-guided fuzzing of closed-source Windows binaries is difficult. WinAFL relies on dynamic instrumentation that slows execution, earlier static rewriting tools need full symbols, and hardware-assisted Intel PT approaches struggled inside virtual machines. The speaker built PEAFL, a tool that statically rewrites PE files by duplicating an executable section, inserting coverage code there, appending a section for the coverage bitmap, and repairing headers, relocations and jump targets.

The hardest problem is separating code from data in the executable section when no symbols exist. Misread data gets instrumented and corrupted, while missed code leaves branches pointing at stale addresses. The speaker used a semi-automated approach that validates branch targets and fixes remaining cases by hand. On a GDI+ benchmark in a Windows 10 virtual machine, the rewritten binary ran about twice as fast as under WinAFL, with overhead around double native execution. A demo kernel driver with a planted crash was fuzzed live. Case studies included a kernel driver with an undocumented format, where patching a checksum helped find crashes, a CNG driver that needed valid object headers in its inputs, and registry hive fuzzing across the whole kernel, which required skipping a self-modifying branch.

The talk closes by arguing that static instrumentation delivers speed but is not a clean or reliable approach, with missing symbols as the main obstacle. The same rewriting can feed back more than coverage, such as memory or stack state for finding uninitialized variables, and it applies beyond fuzzing to tracing and bug detection. The speaker said the source code would be released later.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2019
talks.teaser: Shows known and new fault injection attacks that bypass embedded secure boot, and how designers can harden boot chains.
talks.summary:
The talk addresses why secure boot remains vulnerable on embedded devices, and aims to give guidance to the people who design its hardware, its software and the products that ship with it. The speakers review public breaks first. One is a bootrom downgrade that replaced a strong signature check with a weak hash that contains no secrets. Another is a buffer overflow in a USB recovery mode that could be exploited with ordinary software techniques. The rest are fault injection bypasses of hash and length checks on a game console and a handheld. They note that many boot implementations lack basic exploit mitigations and that the attack surface is often larger than assumed.

They then present attacks they describe as new. The first targets one-time programmable memory. Its configuration flags are copied into shadow registers by hardware before the CPU leaves reset, so a glitch during that transfer can flip a secure boot enable bit before any code runs. The second shows that encrypting the second-stage bootloader does not stop a glitch attack. A plaintext payload is laid out with a sled of pointers, and a glitch that corrupts a load during the copy can send the program counter into the injected image, skipping decryption and verification without a key. A live demonstration on an STM32 target, driven by a fault injector and a Python framework, reported around 260 successful bypasses in about an hour over roughly 9,000 experiments.

For practitioners, the takeaways are to keep boot designs simple, limit the algorithm choices an attacker can pick, and authenticate code and data before using them. Designers should drop privileges where feasible, make fixes possible in the field, and block rollback to vulnerable versions. Fault effects are hard to predict from paper reviews, so the speakers recommend testing hardware directly with fault injection as part of a secure development lifecycle.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2019 - Or Pinchasof - Bridging Emulation and the Real World with the Nintendo Game Boy
talks.teaser: Shows how a Game Boy Advance link protocol was sniffed, reverse engineered and emulated to trade Pokémon with a PC.
talks.summary:
The talk traces a project from around 2005 to connect a Game Boy Advance to a PC, so that Pokémon Ruby and Sapphire could be traded with a version the speaker did not have access to. It starts with the console's two linking modes, multi-pak and single-pak multiboot, and with the physical link cable, whose data lines carry bit-level serial transfers at about 115,200 bits per second. A logic analyzer and an Arduino sniffer captured real transfers, and reading the BIOS and game code against hardware specification documents revealed the multiboot stages: probing, header, a simple key exchange, the data transfer, and a checksum before execution on the slave.

Next, the speaker built an Arduino-based interface that let a PC push code into a second console, then integrated the link logic into the Visual Boy Advance emulator. Trades failed because USB serial latency pushed transfers outside the timing the game expected. Moving the code to a Raspberry Pi with direct GPIO access, dedicating a CPU core to the emulator, and tuning timing and frame throttling reduced the delay to almost nothing. Custom test software run on real hardware was used to compare the emulator's register state and timing against the console.

The live demonstrations were only partly successful: multiplayer loading in single-pak mode worked, but Pokémon trades were sensitive to delay. The main takeaway is that an embedded system like this exposes every layer, from bit timing to game logic, and that newer hardware or interfaces do not always beat older direct port access.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2018 - Lee Holmes - How to Design a New Cloud Platform with a Strong Security Posture
talks.teaser: Describes how Azure Stack was hardened by default, with sealed hosts, constrained operator access and tightly scoped identities.
talks.summary:
The talk covers how Microsoft designed Azure Stack, a hybrid cloud platform that brings Azure services on-premises for disconnected sites, regulated environments and legacy hardware. Earlier attempts fell short: the Windows Azure Pack relied on lengthy hardening guides that customers might skip, and the Cloud Platform System showed that a validated whole system carries risks its individual components do not.

Design decisions followed from that. Hosts are sealed so customers have no fabric access, secure boot and TPM 2.0 form a hardware root of trust, and the baseline builds on Windows Server features such as credential protection, code integrity and Device Guard. Service credentials rotate daily through group managed service accounts kept out of domain admin groups. Operators use a privileged endpoint whose support access needs a two-phase unlock involving Microsoft, and every session is logged. Network whitelisting at switches, software-defined networking and host firewalls limits lateral movement, while controllers use Just Enough Administration instead of WMI-based admin interfaces.

The closing section covers audit policy and central event collection, a cloud controls matrix assessment, and vendor threat modeling and independent pen tests. One vendor's pen test found flawed firmware and overflow bugs in open-source components, which were fixed upstream. The takeaway is to use built-in platform features, accept the engineering work that hard fixes need, and refuse requests that weaken the design.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2018 - Mathy Vanhoef - KRACKing WPA2 in Practice Using Key Reinstallation Attacks
talks.teaser: Explains how key reinstallation flaws in the WPA2 four-way handshake let attackers decrypt and replay Wi-Fi traffic.
talks.summary:
The talk examines a flaw in WPA2 found in the four-way handshake, the exchange where a client and access point prove they share a password and derive a fresh session key. The speaker explains how that key is then used with a per-frame packet counter, which only stays secure if the counter is never reused under the same key.

The attack tricks a client into reinstalling a key it already holds. An attacker relaying traffic on a rogue channel drops the final handshake message, prompting a retransmitted message three that resets the counter. Reused counters then let captured frames be decrypted and replayed. With CCMP that is the limit, though TKIP and GCMP would also allow forgery. Some implementations were vulnerable and others were not, and a Linux and Android supplicant could be made to install an all-zero key.

The practical advice centers on patching both clients and access points, since patching one leaves the other exposed. Access points can shield unpatched clients by not retransmitting message three. The talk also corrects myths, such as the idea that attackers must be nearby or know the password. It closes with disclosure lessons: formal proofs do not guarantee that code matches its model, and multi-party disclosures should prepare for leaks.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2018 - Matt Tait - Keynote: Fake News and Info-Ops: Modern Information Warfare…
talks.teaser: Traces information warfare from ancient propaganda and Soviet forgeries to modern leaks, social media floods and deepfakes.
talks.summary:
Matt Tait opens this BlueHat Israel 2018 keynote by arguing that fake news and disinformation are old problems rather than a novelty of 2017. He separates disinformation, which deliberately misleads, from misinformation, which is an honest mistake, and explains why people accept facts that match their existing views. Tribalism and confirmation bias make that worse. He illustrates the pattern with Ramesses II's self-glorifying account of the battle of Kadesh and Octavian's allegedly forged will of Mark Antony, which was used to justify war.

He then moves to the Cold War, citing 1982 congressional testimony that put Soviet active measures at about three billion dollars a year. Forged telegrams in India, Nigeria and Greece were used to stir unrest and mistrust. He then covers modern operations: the 2014 hack of Ukraine's election commission, which published a false winner before officials took the site down, the takeover of the TV5Monde broadcaster, and the DNC leaks, where two releases of the same emails differed in edits, exposing forgery. He also describes WikiLeaks-style daily dumps that flooded the news cycle and divisive issues such as Black Lives Matter, used to split society.

Looking ahead, Tait warns of convincing deepfakes, ransomware that could leak stolen data as pressure, and influence campaigns run by non-state groups. His proposed responses include tamper-proof metadata that reveals edited documents, relying on primary sources rather than asking users to judge truth, reputation-based automated moderation, and social tools that expose people to opposing views.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2018 - Marina Simakov & Itai Grady
talks.teaser: Shows how attackers abuse Active Directory computer accounts across recon, lateral movement and persistence, while staying hidden.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that attackers concentrate on user and service accounts, while computer accounts get far less monitoring and can still be turned into a powerful foothold in an Active Directory domain. The speakers walk through how these accounts can be abused at each stage of an intrusion. During reconnaissance, an attacker can look for computer accounts that were created with empty passwords by some provisioning tools, either by testing logons or by requesting service tickets and trying to decrypt them. For lateral movement, a compromised computer account can be used to open a secure channel on behalf of a target server, which yields the session key needed to sign traffic and get past SMB signing during relay attacks.

For persistence, the presenters show how a relayed administrative LDAP session can be used to set delegation on a computer account, so that it can request service tickets for other users, including domain administrators, against a chosen service. To avoid detection, they add access control entries that deny read access to the delegation-related attributes, so the account looks ordinary to anyone querying the directory. Because no physical machine is attached, its password never rotates, so the access persists. A live demo runs through the relay, the attribute changes and the hiding step.

For defenders, the mitigations include scanning for computer accounts with empty or weak passwords, monitoring bursts of ticket requests and logon operations from one machine, auditing delegation settings, and marking privileged accounts as sensitive and not delegable. To find objects hidden through access control, the speakers compare results from LSA SID lookups with standard LDAP queries. Their takeaway is that computer accounts belong in the same monitoring scope as privileged user accounts.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2018 - Oran Avraham - eMMC Hacking, Or: How I Fixed Long-Dead Galaxy S3 Phones
talks.teaser: Shows how a faulty eMMC storage chip bricked Galaxy S3 phones and how the speaker recovered them.
talks.summary:
Around 2012, Galaxy S3 phones began failing without warning in a problem called sudden death syndrome. Samsung released a kernel patch in the MMC subsystem, and the speaker studied it to understand the cause. The patch contained a hidden backdoor sequence built from manufacturer-reserved commands, and an odd erase call. Using that backdoor, the speaker dumped the firmware running inside the chip's controller.

Analysis of the dumped firmware showed the root cause. The flash translation layer wrote a miscalculated value into its metadata, and the default exception handler then looped forever, so the chip stopped responding at boot. Samsung's patch avoided triggering the bug rather than fixing it. To recover bricked phones, the speaker used a bootloader flaw reachable over USB, with out-of-bounds read and write bugs left unpatched on the S3. When the boot partition was corrupt, the phone could load the bootloader from an external SD card instead. Interrupting the chip's boot within a 35 millisecond window forced it into its boot ROM, where new firmware could be flashed and the metadata reformatted.

The talk closes with early work on newer eMMC chips, tested on a development board, where a comparable vendor command returned a firmware image. The main takeaway is that eMMC is NAND flash behind a controller with its own firmware, and hidden vendor commands can expose that firmware to recovery and analysis.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2017 - Marina Simakov & Tal Be'ery - The Enemy Within...
talks.teaser: Shows how shared local administrator accounts create hidden lateral movement paths in Windows networks, and how to detect them.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how local Windows accounts, whose password hashes sit in the local SAM database, can be abused during lateral movement. The speakers argue that local authentication gets less attention than domain credentials, and that identical local administrator passwords across domain machines turn a network into one where any compromised host reaches all the others. They also cover risks from local users defined through old group policy preferences and from enabled guest accounts.

The live demo follows an attacker who compromises one domain account and brute-forces a local administrator password with a custom tool that works locally, so it avoids network monitoring. The attacker then dumps the local hashes, queries other machines for their local administrators using ordinary domain-user rights, and runs code remotely with pass-the-hash. On the compromised host, the attacker can also add a backdoor user to the administrators group and strip domain admins of their rights.

For defenders, the speakers present Local Hero, a scanner that runs from a separate machine without installing agents. It collects local users and group memberships remotely and flags dormant accounts that suddenly log on, brute-force indicators, privileged group changes, enabled guest accounts, and cloned accounts that share an exact password-set timestamp. Recommended hardening includes restricting remote SAM queries, denying remote access for local accounts through group policy, and rotating unique local administrator passwords with LAPS.

talks.title: Think Next 2016- Jasmin Fisher, Senior Researcher, Microsoft Research
talks.teaser: Shows how executable biology models built like software help predict cancer drug resistance and tailor glioblastoma treatment.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the question of why cancer remains so hard to solve. The speaker explains that cells are complex systems of many interacting molecules, genes and proteins, and that cancer has no fixed plan; it evolves and reacts to genetics and environment. The proposed answer is an approach called executable biology, developed over about twelve years in a Cambridge research group. It treats biological processes as computer programs and applies formal verification, the same kind of checking used for software and hardware, to confirm they behave as intended.

The speaker described how computational models are built to mimic cellular processes and are then compared with laboratory observations, which reveals gaps in what is understood about a mechanism. A graphical, drag-and-drop tool developed at Microsoft Research lets biologists who are not professional programmers build and explore these models. One leukemia model predicted new drug combinations that could overcome drug resistance. In work with a pharmaceutical company, models built from patient-specific clinical data produced predictions that were then checked experimentally on the same patients' cell samples. For glioblastoma, a simulated tumour can test chemotherapy and radiotherapy options in minutes, whereas dish-based testing can take weeks or months.

The main takeaway is that such models can reveal the drivers and bottlenecks of cancer, which might be targeted across different cancer types and used to support personalised treatment. The speaker does not claim cancer will be eradicated outright, but expects that within ten years, using these technologies, the problem will be considered solved.

talks.title: Think Next 2016- Gerald Jay Sanders, CEO, SkyTran Inc.
talks.teaser: Presents SkyTran, an elevated magnetic transport system pitched as a low-cost, low-energy answer to urban traffic congestion.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the argument that traffic is getting worse as car ownership grows in fast-developing regions, and that building more roads only draws more cars onto them. The speaker presents SkyTran, an elevated transport system that runs above surface traffic on a slim guideway held up by a small pole. He claims it costs far less to build and run than light rail or a bullet train, and uses less energy than a hybrid car.

To explain how the vehicle lifts, the speaker runs a hand demonstration with a magnet dropped over a plastic sheet and then over an aluminum one. Over aluminum the magnet slows sharply because induced currents in the metal resist it, which he compares to the braking of a roller coaster. Pairs of angled magnets, which he calls magnetic wings, produce the same effect, and a small glider and a vehicle model rise off the track once pulled forward. Propulsion comes from a rotary magnetic motor inside an aluminum sleeve.

The speaker says the project is a NASA Space Act company based at Ames Research Center, developed with Israel Aerospace Industries. It has moved from subscale models to a full-size demonstration system under construction in Israel, with a test vehicle already running on its guideway. He says the system can reach about 240 km/h, skip stations to follow a set schedule, and that several cities have requested systems.
